solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Seated, is given food around one, making one this? (9)

annotation.definition: Seated, is given food around one, making one this?

indicatorNotes.around: FED is placed around the letter, surrounding it on both sides

annotation.surface: Someone sits down at the table and is served a meal.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the wordplay: someone seated and fed ends up this, so the last words only make sense after the rest. The two 'one's are separate words doing separate jobs.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by consequence: being sat down and well fed is what leaves a person content, so the clue's 'this' is the state the meal produces.

entries.clue: Stunted growth in small vineyard with beginning of blight (5)

indicatorNotes.beginning of: the beginning of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels
a cru is a French vineyard or its wine

annotation.surface: A small vineyard whose vines are stunted by blight.
annotation.walkthrough: CRU is a wine-list word worth knowing: a vineyard, as in grand cru. 'Growth' also fits the wine world, where a cru is sometimes called a growth.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: scrub is the low, stunted bushes and trees of poor ground, growth that never reaches full height.

entries.clue: Nominate Hamlet in the press for classic book (3,8,6)

indicatorNotes.in: PICK and WICK sit in THE PAPERS, enclosed by it

blocks.note: a wick is a hamlet, as in place names like Warwick

annotation.surface: Someone nominates Shakespeare's Hamlet in the newspapers as a classic.
annotation.walkthrough: Hamlet looks like the play, which suits a clue about classic books; here it is a small village, WICK.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Dickens's first novel is one of the standard classics of English literature.

entries.clue: Keep quiet about my family’s Douglas making bread (9)

indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so SH goes round the rest

blocks.note: what belongs to my family is ours

annotation.surface: A family asks someone to stay silent about their relative Douglas's baking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My family's' asks for a possessive, and the family speaking would say 'our'. The name Douglas is cut to its usual short form.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: sourdough is bread leavened with a fermented starter rather than yeast.

entries.clue: Writer’s vessel has American turtle avoiding strait (6)

indicatorNotes.avoiding: the turtle keeps clear of the strait, so those letters are left out

blocks.note: the stinkpot is a North American musk turtle
St = strait, as on maps; removed from the front

annotation.surface: An author's ship carries an American turtle but steers clear of a narrow channel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a ship, which is why the strait fits the picture; it is a pot. The stinkpot turtle is obscure, but INK and POT together make the answer easy to check.
annotation.definitionFit: Vessel in its container sense: an inkpot is the small pot a writer dips a pen into.

entries.clue: Belittling awful creep during romantic activity (11)

indicatorNotes.awful: something awful is in a bad state, so the letters are knocked out of shape
indicatorNotes.during: the creep happens during the dating, so it sits inside that word

annotation.surface: Someone is dismissive about a horrible creep met while dating.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface describes a bad date, and the answer describes how you might talk about it afterwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: deprecating remarks run something down, which is belittling it.

entries.clue: Funny man embraced by achiever’s widow (7)

indicatorNotes.embraced by: whatever is embraced is held inside the arms of the other word

blocks.note: a doer is someone who gets things done

annotation.surface: A comedian is hugged by the widow of a successful man.
annotation.walkthrough: The possessive makes 'achiever's widow' read as one phrase, but the widow stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A narrower sense: a dowager is specifically a widow holding a title or property from her late husband.

entries.clue: Approach doctor with bristle on lughole (4,4)

blocks.note: an awn is the bristle on an ear of barley
lughole is British slang for ear

annotation.surface: Someone goes up to a doctor about a hair growing on their ear.
annotation.walkthrough: AWN is a crossword regular: the stiff bristle on grasses such as barley. 'Approach' looks like a verb addressed to the doctor, and it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, a rather literary one: to draw near is to come closer, to approach.

entries.clue: Show how, when formatted, this list shows names at the top (4,3)

annotation.definition: this list shows names at the top

indicatorNotes.when formatted: formatting rearranges text into a new layout, so the letters are laid out afresh

annotation.surface: Instructions on formatting a list so the names appear at the top.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At the top' reads as page layout, which fits 'formatted'; it means people at the top of society.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: Who's Who is the reference book of prominent people, so its names are those of people at the top.

entries.clue: Unnatural quality of entertainer with part in G&S (11)

indicatorNotes.in: the entertainer and his part sit in G&S, between the two letters

blocks.note: Gilbert and Sullivan, reduced to initials
an actor's part is their lines

annotation.surface: A performer with a role in a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta.
annotation.walkthrough: G&S is Gilbert and Sullivan, the Victorian comic-opera partnership; here they just supply the outer G and S.
annotation.definitionFit: Unnatural in the sense of supernatural: ghostliness is the eerie quality of something not of this world.

entries.clue: Applying block, is getting brown during time off (9)

indicatorNotes.during: the tanning happens during the time off, so it sits inside REST

annotation.surface: Someone puts on sunblock while getting a tan on holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Block' looks like sunblock, which fits the tanning; it means resistance, putting up a block.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: someone who puts a block in the way of something is resistant to it, as sunblock resists the sun.

entries.clue: Timeless photo capturing a king in military headgear (5)

indicatorNotes.Timeless: without time, so the T for time goes
indicatorNotes.capturing: the photo takes the letters prisoner, holding them inside

annotation.surface: An old photograph of a king wearing an army hat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Timeless' suggests a classic photo; here it simply strips a T.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by type: a shako is the tall, peaked, plumed cap of nineteenth-century soldiers.

entries.clue: Disease of, namely, fir tree genus (7)

blocks.note: Abies is the Latin genus of firs

annotation.surface: A disease that afflicts fir trees.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a tree disease; scabies is a human skin one. SC for namely comes from Latin scilicet.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: scabies is the itching skin disease caused by burrowing mites.

entries.clue: Ship new type of gas (5)

annotation.surface: A new kind of fuel for shipping.
annotation.walkthrough: The Argo is the crossword's favourite ship, carrying Jason and the Argonauts.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: argon is one of the noble gases, the inert kind that fills light bulbs.

entries.clue: Fair then bad in school exam (2,3,5)

indicatorNotes.bad: a bad version of the word is a spoilt one, its letters jumbled
indicatorNotes.in: the jumbled word goes in the exam, between O and LEVEL

blocks.note: O level, the old British school exam taken at about sixteen

annotation.surface: A pupil's exam result goes from fair to bad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fair then bad' reads like exam grades; 'Fair' is the definition. An O level was the British exam at sixteen, replaced by GCSEs.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone on the level is honest and above board, which is fair dealing.

entries.clue: Take over a thousand solid gold deer (7)

indicatorNotes.Take over: to take something over is to turn it over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a cube is a solid shape

annotation.surface: An instruction to seize more than a thousand pounds' worth of gold deer figures.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Take over a thousand' reads as 'more than a thousand'; 'Take over' is the whole instruction, and everything after it is the wordplay until the deer.
annotation.definitionFit: A narrower term: a roebuck is the male of the roe, a small European deer.

entries.clue: Joanna has quiet man round (5)

annotation.surface: Joanna is with a quiet man who is round.
annotation.walkthrough: Joanna is Cockney rhyming slang for piano, and it looks like a woman's name. P for quiet comes from the same Italian musical term as the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: in Cockney rhyming slang a joanna is a piano, from the way 'piano' sounds in a Cockney accent.

entries.clue: Lots are in stitches with tons delayed in fierce attack (9)

indicatorNotes.delayed: the T is held back and arrives last
indicatorNotes.in: LAUGH goes into the rearranged word

blocks.note: TONS with the T moved to the end
to be in stitches is to laugh
surface subject: the lots are the tons that go on to be rearranged

annotation.surface: A lot of people are laughing hard.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lots' and 'tons' are the same thing, and the T of those tons comes late so LAUGH can slot in before it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an onslaught is a violent, overwhelming attack.

entries.clue: I bewitch with melodic nonsense, somehow get confused (5,7,4,7)

indicatorNotes.somehow: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters come out in some other order

annotation.surface: A singer boasts of enchanting listeners with tuneful gibberish.
annotation.walkthrough: The 23 letters of I BEWITCH and MELODIC NONSENSE rearrange; 'with' only joins them.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to blind someone with science is to baffle them with technical talk, getting them confused.

entries.clue: Ship’s track visible after daybreak in surface? (4,2)

blocks.note: the wake is the trail a ship leaves
the sun is up after daybreak

annotation.surface: A ship's trail showing on the sea's surface at dawn.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Surface' looks like the sea's surface; it is the verb, to come up from sleep.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: people who surface in the morning come up out of sleep as a diver comes up out of water.

entries.clue: Anger with engaging artist for one (5)

indicatorNotes.engaging: to engage is to take on, so WITH takes the artist on board
indicatorNotes.for: for as in instead of: the artist stands in for the one

blocks.note: I = one, the letter RA replaces

annotation.surface: Rage at hiring an artist, for one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For one' reads as 'for example'; it means RA goes in place of one (I).
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with extra force: wrath is fierce, often righteous anger.

entries.clue: Actress Leslie’s mother, perhaps one who cares about their appearance (8)

annotation.definitionNote: 'one' does double duty: 'one who cares about their appearance'
annotation.surface: Leslie Caron's mother, a woman who always looked immaculate.
annotation.walkthrough: The possessive puts Caron's MA first. The answer is not pasta but the 18th-century dandy, the one in Yankee Doodle.
annotation.definitionFit: A historical sense: a macaroni was an 18th-century English fop who dressed in extravagant continental fashion.

entries.clue: Free muscles needing source of oil without iodine (7)

indicatorNotes.without: without means lacking, so the iodine is taken out

blocks.note: olive oil comes from the olive
I is the chemical symbol for iodine, removed

annotation.surface: Loosening tight muscles needs oil, but not iodine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Free' looks like an adjective about muscles; it is the verb, to clear of blame.
annotation.definitionFit: A narrower sense: to absolve is to free someone from guilt, blame or an obligation.

entries.clue: Shun holiday walking in Antarctica? (5,3,2,3,4)

blocks.note: anyone walking there is out in the cold

annotation.surface: Avoiding a holiday spent trekking across Antarctica.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second half: a polar walker is literally out in the cold.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: leaving someone out in the cold means excluding them from a group, a way of shunning them.

entries.clue: Choose sulphur to put in (6)

blocks.note: to elect is to vote someone in

annotation.surface: Deciding whether to add sulphur.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put in' is the voting sense: to put someone in office.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, and the answer contains its near-twin ELECT, which also means to choose.

entries.clue: Calculating crime that I arranged (10)

indicatorNotes.arranged: arranged means put in order, here a new order

annotation.surface: A cunning criminal confesses to planning an offence.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Calculating' looks like an adjective for a scheming criminal; it is the noun, sums.
annotation.definitionFit: Calculating read as a noun: arithmetic is the working out of sums with numbers.

entries.clue: Kind to have an impact on island edges in tide (12)

indicatorNotes.edges in: the edges of a word are its outside letters

blocks.note: to affect = to have an impact on

annotation.surface: The tide lapping around the edges of an island.
annotation.walkthrough: Iona is a small island off western Scotland, a regular in crosswords.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: kind and affectionate both describe warm, loving treatment of others.

entries.clue: Wasted payment on French corn (6)

blocks.note: blé is French for wheat, corn

annotation.surface: Money thrown away on buying French grain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wasted' reads as squandered, fitting the payment; it means weak and feeble.
annotation.definitionFit: Wasted in its bodily sense: a body wasted by illness has lost its strength.

entries.clue: Route diverted further from the centre (5)

indicatorNotes.diverted: a diverted road takes a different course, and so do the letters

annotation.surface: A road rerouted away from the town centre.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a traffic diversion, and the answer belongs to the same picture of ring roads.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description: the outer part of anything lies further out than its middle.

entries.clue: Frontage a shop can install above on opening (6)

annotation.definition: Frontage a shop can install above on opening

indicatorNotes.on opening: each word is taken on its opening, its first letter

blocks.clueFragment: Frontage a shop can install above
blocks.note: the opening letter of each word

annotation.surface: A shopfitter's advice on putting up a sign over a shop's entrance.
annotation.walkthrough: The first word of the clue both defines and starts the spelling, and 'on opening' sounds like a shop's opening day.
annotation.definitionFit: A specialised sense: a fascia is the name board across a shopfront, the frontage passers-by read.

entries.clue: One rambling president splitting House of Representatives (5)

indicatorNotes.splitting: the president splits the pair of letters by coming between them

annotation.surface: A long-winded president divides the US House of Representatives.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rambling' suggests talking too long in Congress; it means walking in the countryside.
annotation.definitionFit: Rambling in its walking sense: a hiker is out on a long country walk, which the British call a ramble.

entries.clue: University in middle of Mercia is concerned with spelling (5)

indicatorNotes.in: the university goes in the middle letters
indicatorNotes.middle of: the middle of a word is its central letters

blocks.note: the two middle letters of meRCia

annotation.surface: A university in the English Midlands takes spelling seriously.
annotation.walkthrough: Mercia was an Anglo-Saxon kingdom in central England. 'Spelling' looks like orthography; it means casting spells, and runes carried magic.
annotation.definitionFit: A punning sense: runes were used in charms, so runic writing was concerned with spells as well as letters.

entries.clue: English roar for score (7)

annotation.surface: English fans roaring for a goal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Score' looks like a goal to cheer; it means to cut lines into a surface.
annotation.definitionFit: Score in its cutting sense: scoring and engraving both scratch lines into a hard surface.

entries.clue: Very surprised was leading immediately after kick-off (8)

indicatorNotes.immediately after: one piece follows straight on from the other

annotation.surface: A team goes ahead straight after the match starts.
annotation.walkthrough: The football surface reads as one sentence about an early goal, and the result is the crowd's reaction.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with a jolt in it: to be startled is to be suddenly and sharply surprised.

entries.clue: Sudden game point after a bye (6)

indicatorNotes.after: the game and point come after the other pieces

annotation.surface: A game suddenly decided by a point after one side got a bye.
annotation.walkthrough: RU for rugby union and B for bye, a cricket extra, are standard.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something abrupt happens without warning, like a sudden stop.

entries.clue: Magazine to quote Newton over demonstrating attraction (8)

indicatorNotes.over: turned over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: N = newton, the unit of force

annotation.surface: A science magazine quotes Isaac Newton on gravity.
annotation.walkthrough: Newton suggests gravitational attraction, which is apt, but he contributes only N.
annotation.definitionFit: Both literal and figurative: magnets attract iron, and a magnetic personality attracts people.

entries.clue: Mistake about mostly doubtful hour’s suspense at end of programme (11)

indicatorNotes.about: the mistake goes about, around, the other letters
indicatorNotes.mostly: most of the word, so the last letter goes

annotation.surface: A dubious hour of television ends with a blunder.
annotation.walkthrough: A clanger is British slang for a blunder, from dropping something with a clang.
annotation.definitionFit: A description of the device: a cliffhanger leaves the story unresolved so viewers come back for the next episode.

entries.clue: Vehicle reinforced by aged tungsten in conflict (4,3)

indicatorNotes.reinforced by: the car is filled out from within by the other letters

blocks.note: W is the chemical symbol for tungsten

annotation.surface: An armoured vehicle strengthened with old tungsten for battle.
annotation.walkthrough: The military surface of armour and battle keeps the answer's war in view throughout.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Cold War was the decades-long standoff between the West and the Soviet bloc.

entries.clue: Hardly pausing to avoid the risk of work after card game (7-4)

indicatorNotes.after: the other pieces come after the card game

blocks.note: lest = so as to avoid the risk

annotation.surface: Card players barely stop so they don't have to go to work.
annotation.walkthrough: A whistle-stop tour makes only brief stops, as trains once did at small stations.
annotation.definitionFit: From American railways: a whistle-stop was a tiny halt where trains paused briefly, so a whistle-stop tour hardly pauses anywhere.

entries.clue: Convex floor’s not good (5)

indicatorNotes.not: the floor is 'not good', so the G for good is removed

annotation.surface: A curved floor is no good.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not good' reads as a verdict on the floor; it is the instruction to lose G.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: a convex surface bulges outwards, curved and round like the outside of a ball.

entries.clue: Child’s pet is unreliable, but grand for second daughter (5)

indicatorNotes.for: for as in instead of: grand goes in place of the daughter

blocks.note: the second D in DODGY is swapped out

annotation.surface: A child's pet is unpredictable, but grand compared with a younger daughter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second daughter' reads as a younger child in the family; it means the second D in DODGY.
annotation.definitionFit: A nursery word: doggy is how small children name a dog.

entries.clue: Five tangling with Balrog such as may be let go (10)

annotation.definition: such as may be let go

indicatorNotes.tangling with: letters that tangle get knotted into a new order

annotation.surface: Five people fight a Balrog, the fire demon in Tolkien, and it lets them go.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Five' tempts you to use V; the word is taken whole.
annotation.definitionFit: Let go in the sense of overlooked: a forgivable fault is one that can be pardoned and dropped.

entries.clue: Too desperately ill for forty-one? (12)

blocks.note: a critical patient is desperately ill

annotation.surface: Someone far too sick for their age of forty-one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Forty-one' reads as an age; it points to the answer at 41 across, NITPICKING.
annotation.definitionFit: A cross-reference: the answer at 41 across is NITPICKING, and nitpickers find fault too readily.

entries.clue: Funny feeling with home teaching (9)

annotation.surface: An odd sensation about home schooling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Funny' means strange here, not amusing.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a funny feeling is a hunch you cannot explain, which is what intuition supplies.

entries.clue: On reflection, can picture monarch finding fault (10)

indicatorNotes.On reflection: a reflection in a mirror shows things backwards

annotation.surface: After thinking it over, someone can imagine a king criticising.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb; it is a tin. 'On reflection' turns only the tin.
annotation.definitionFit: A narrower sense: nitpicking is fault-finding over tiny details, like picking nits from hair.

entries.clue: Bird circling unfortunately cut person waving stick (9)

indicatorNotes.circling: the bird flies round the other letters, enclosing them
indicatorNotes.unfortunately: something that fares unfortunately goes wrong, and the letters go out of order

annotation.surface: A bird flying in circles, sadly injured.
annotation.walkthrough: The stick is a baton, not something a bird carries.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a conductor leads an orchestra by waving a baton, the stick of the clue.

entries.clue: Weep about Stan’s partner and mine (8)

indicatorNotes.about: the weeping goes about, around, the partner

blocks.note: Oliver Hardy, partner of Stan Laurel

annotation.surface: Crying over Laurel and Hardy, and over what belongs to me.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mine' looks like a possessive; it is a coal mine.
annotation.definitionFit: A narrower term: a colliery is a coal mine together with its buildings.

entries.clue: Suggest altering partly psychological concept (7)

indicatorNotes.partly: only part of the phrase is used, the answer lying inside it

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

annotation.surface: A therapist proposes changing a theory.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Altering' tempts you towards an anagram; the answer lies in plain sight across the word break.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Gestalt psychology holds that we perceive wholes that are more than the sum of their parts.

entries.clue: Child that’s taken on song and dance part on the stage finally (7)

indicatorNotes.finally: finally points to the last letter of each word

blocks.note: a song and dance is a fuss, ado
last letters of thE and stagE

annotation.surface: A child actor given a singing and dancing role in a stage show.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Song and dance' looks theatrical; it means a fuss, ADO.
annotation.definitionFit: Taken on in the sense of taken in as family: an adoptee is a child legally made someone else's own.

entries.clue: Hot roofs unfortunately aged indeed (8)

indicatorNotes.unfortunately: things that turn out unfortunately go wrong, and the letters go out of order

annotation.surface: Roofs overheating have sadly aged.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Aged' marks the definition as old-fashioned language.
annotation.definitionFit: An archaic word: forsooth is the old way of saying 'indeed', so it is an aged indeed.

entries.clue: Run a social engagement around one in shed (7)

indicatorNotes.around: the date goes around the one, enclosing it

blocks.note: a date is a social engagement

annotation.surface: Hosting a get-together in a garden shed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shed' looks like the garden building; it is the verb, to give off.
annotation.definitionFit: Shed in the sense of give off: a lamp sheds light, which is to radiate it.

entries.clue: Turkey gutted after bird is difficult (6)

indicatorNotes.gutted: a gutted bird has its insides removed, leaving only the outer letters
indicatorNotes.after: the turkey's remains come after the bird

blocks.note: the knot is a wading bird

annotation.surface: Preparing a turkey after dealing with another bird is hard work.
annotation.walkthrough: The knot is a crossword-favourite shore bird.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: a knotty problem is as hard to work out as a tangled knot is to undo.

entries.clue: Mostly kind about ram’s dazed state (6)

indicatorNotes.Mostly: most of the word, so the last letter goes
indicatorNotes.about: the shortened word goes about, around, the ram

annotation.surface: A ram, mostly gentle, is in a daze.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Kind' looks like an adjective for the ram; it is the noun, a sort.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a stupor is a state of near-unconsciousness where the mind is dazed.

entries.clue: Sadly bemoan culture drama with visit here? (8,3,6,6)

annotation.definition: Sadly bemoan culture drama with visit here?

indicatorNotes.Sadly: things that go sadly go badly, and the letters go wrong

annotation.surface: Someone laments cultural drama and suggests a trip to a museum.
annotation.walkthrough: The V&A is London's museum of art and design, a place to visit for culture. 'With' joins the two parts of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: An &lit: the whole clue reads as a suggestion for someone fed up with culture to visit the V&A, a great London museum of design.

entries.clue: Section of sacred opus? (5)

indicatorNotes.Section of: only a section of the phrase is used, the answer lying inside it

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

annotation.surface: A movement from a piece of sacred music.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: the Credo is a section of the sung Mass.
annotation.definitionFit: An &lit: the Credo, the creed, is one movement of a musical setting of the Mass, a sacred opus.

entries.clue: Southern English after staff for northern vicarage (5)

indicatorNotes.after: the southern and English letters come after the staff

annotation.surface: A southern Englishman looking for staff for a vicarage up north.
annotation.walkthrough: A manse is a minister's house, especially in Scotland, hence 'northern'.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: manse is the Scottish word for a minister's house, the northern counterpart of a vicarage.

entries.clue: Swimming in the sea around reef regularly using a snorkel? (9)

indicatorNotes.around: the swimming goes around the reef's letters
indicatorNotes.regularly: at regular intervals, so every other letter

annotation.surface: Swimming in the sea over a reef with a snorkel.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: a snorkel lets you keep breathing with your face in the water.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a snorkel is a tube whose whole purpose is to let a swimmer draw air.

entries.clue: Green comes after a stop (5)

indicatorNotes.comes after: the green follows on after the A

annotation.surface: A traffic light goes green after the stop signal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stop' looks like a traffic signal; it is the verb, to prevent.
annotation.definitionFit: Stop in the sense of prevent: averting a disaster keeps it from ever happening.

entries.clue: Criticise record (3,4)

blocks.note: to put someone down is to belittle them
to put something down is to write it on paper

annotation.surface: An order to criticise the minutes of a meeting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Record' looks like a noun, a disc or a best time; it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses of one phrasal verb: a put-down is a cutting remark, and putting something down in writing records it.

entries.clue: Call out first woman that’s permitted inside (5)

indicatorNotes.inside: the permission goes inside the woman's name

blocks.note: Eve, the first woman in Genesis

annotation.surface: Summoning Eve, who is allowed into the garden.
annotation.walkthrough: 'First woman' is Eve by long crossword habit, from the Book of Genesis.
annotation.definitionFit: An older sense: to evoke originally meant to call out or summon a spirit, and now to call up a feeling.

entries.clue: Plant provider’s charge over Southeastern Railway (7)

indicatorNotes.over: turned over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to charge is to run at something

annotation.surface: A garden centre's delivery fee for goods sent by Southeastern, a train company in south-east England.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Charge' looks like a fee in this commercial surface; it is the verb, to rush forward.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: a nursery grows young plants and sells them to gardeners.

entries.clue: Bird droppings over plaster walls (9)

indicatorNotes.over: turned over, so the letters run backwards
indicatorNotes.walls: the plaster walls in the droppings, surrounding them

blocks.note: to parge is to plaster a wall

annotation.surface: Bird droppings running down plastered walls.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bird' at the start is the definition, not part of 'bird droppings'. PARGE is a builder's word for rendering a wall.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the partridge is a plump game bird of fields and hedgerows.
